newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-SACCHI ENDS DEBATE, QUITS ITALY JOB FOR AC MILAN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SACCHI ENDS DEBATE, QUITS ITALY JOB FOR AC MILAN.

text.p: Italy soccer coach Arrigo Sacchi, increasingly seen as a lame duck even by his team, has ended months of debate about his future by resigning and returning to AC Milan, the club where he made his name.
"Sacchi returns to Milan," trumpeted the Corriere dello Sport newspaper on Monday. "Sacchi and Milan, today they set off again," commented the mass-circulation Gazzetta dello Sport.
The Italian soccer federation (FIGC) special commissioner Raffaele Pagnozzi said Sacchi had called him shortly before midnight on Sunday to advise him of his decision.
"I can't say no to (owner Silvio) Berlusconi. Milan calls me, I can only resign. Try to understand," the Corriere dello Sport quoted the 50-year-old Sacchi as saying.

Sacchi, who spent five glory years at Milan until his appointment to the national side in 1991, replaces Oscar Washington Tabarez who has had a bleak six months with the club that lost 3-2 in the league at lowly Piacenza on Sunday.
That shock defeat for a wealthy club packed with hugely expensive foreign talent was ironically against the only club in serie A without a single non-Italian on its books.
It sent Milan, who have a key Champions' League match against Norway's Rosenborg on Wednesday, down to ninth place in the league table.
Tabarez was the third serie A coach to be fired this season and the second Uruguayan. All three coaches have been foreigners in their first season, all were replaced by Italians.

It was not yet clear who would succeed Sacchi in the most criticised job in Italian soccer but two men have emerged as clear favourites for the nomination, expected after the FIGC elects a new chairman on December 14.
Italy's next match is away to England in February in a key qualifier for the 1998 World Cup. England lead the group although Italy have won both their matches.
The chairman-designate is league president Luciano Nizzola, whose recent public utterances have suggested that Sacchi's days would have been numbered anyway had he wanted to stay.
"Nizzola will now have an embarrassment of choice," commented the Gazzetta dello Sport. "From Maldini, to Zoff, to Scala to Mr X. The hunt is on."

Former World Cup-winning goalkeeper Dino Zoff, now chairman of Lazio, has been heavily tipped as a likely replacement despite a nondescript coaching record, while under-21 coach Cesare Maldini has been seen as a possible stop-gap.
Former Parma coach Nevio Scala is immediately available having left his club at the end of last season.

Other candidates, seemingly coming more from the realms of fantasy football than reality, include Bayern Munich coach Giovanni Trappatoni and Real Madrid coach Fabio Capello -- the man who took over from Sacchi as Milan coach in 1991.
At that time, the national team was held to have rescued Milan from a difficult position by relieving them of Sacchi at a time when several players were openly in revolt.

On Monday, the boot was on the other foot with Milan relieving the FIGC of the need to dismiss a coach whose contract ran to 1998 and who had seemed determined to hang on to the job despite increasing hostility all around him.

Sacchi took Italy to the 1994 World Cup final in Los Angeles, where they lost on penalties to Brazil, but has been under intense pressure since the side crashed out of the European championships in the first round last summer.
His last match in charge was a friendly against Bosnia in Sarajevo last month that Italy lost 2-1.
Sacchi has a record of 34 wins, 10 draws and nine defeats in the 53 matches he has conducted since November 1991.
He has been criticised for frequent change -- trying out almost 100 players in five years -- and falling out with stars, most notably Gianluca Vialli of English club Chelsea.

Soft-spoken, reserved and with his sunglasses almost permanently perched on his forehead, Sacchi divided Italy. Some disliked him so much that they formed an Anti-Sacchi club. Sacchi said he was willing to join too.
